subsubtopic: CALL FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LOAN TO CUBA-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgency stemming from an answer last week to my order paper question concerning the $10 million loan at 3 per cent interest to Cuba approved on February 6, 1975, and the answer stating that to this date no payments have been received on time and that Cuba is currently two semi-annual payments in arrears. I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie):
That this House request a full investigation of this unpaid ridiculous-interest loan presumably inspired by a "viva Castro" spirit, that a demand be made upon the Cuban government to immediately bring its payments up to date, that no further loans at such low interest rates be ever issued when the average Canadian struggles with high interest and mortgage rates and, finally, that the government and Crown corporations cease and desist from making any further loans to extremist governments of the left or right without approval being first given by the Parliament of Canada.

In view of the fact that Trent University, in Peterborough, is now a leading centre for environmental studies in Canada, and because a large amount of office space leased by this government in downtown Peterborough is now vacant because of the cancellation of the Parks Canada regional office in Peterborough, and considering that Peterborough is ideally located among the Kawartha Lakes, and that it is the government's

That this government give immediate consideration to designating Peterborough and Trent University as the centre for environmental research into the acid rain problem, thus taking advantage of an already leased government building in Peterborough, while at the same time recognizing Trent University as a major regional research centre for environmental studies in Canada.

speechtext:

million Canadians who want to work but cannot find employment-almost twice the number of the unemployed during the worst years of the great depression-and given the determination on this side of the House to declare war on the unemployment problem and to have government policies which would create cost-effective real jobs and training opportunities, I move, seconded by the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook):

The House resumed from Wednesday, May 21, consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-16, to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when this bill was under debate on Wednesday, May 21, three of us had spoken to it-the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), the hon. member for Rose-dale (Mr. Crombie) and myself. There is one aspect of this matter which all three of us touched on, namely, the relationship between the amount pensioners have to live on and the level of poverty as established by Statistics Canada.
Those who followed the debate last Wednesday will recall that both of the first two speakers apologized for the fact that pensioners who have to live on old age security and the guaranteed income supplement are being forced to exist on amounts below the recognized poverty level. Incidentally, the

May 26, 1980
Old Age Security Act
poverty level which was talked about last Wednesday is the level established by Statistics Canada, which is the lowest of all the poverty levels which are computed. Indeed, if one looks at the computations of any of the social agencies in any of our larger cities, one finds that the poverty level is much higher.
1 appreciated and understood the apology which the other two speakers made for asking senior citizens to live below the poverty line, but 1 suggested it was not good enough just to try to narrow that gap. The only suggestion made about anyone ever reaching the poverty line was by the minister who thought that possibly by July married couples living in the smaller cities or rural areas would reach the poverty level. I suggested then, and I repeat now, that we should not let this subject of pensions rest until we have established for all our senior citizens a guaranteed level which is above the poverty line. 1 suggested the other day the figure of 125 per cent. One might go higher but one certainly should not go any lower. No longer do we think of pensions as simply a means of keeping older people alive. Surely we have reached the point at which we assert the fact that older people have helped to build the economy and that they have the right in retirement to continue to enjoy the standard of living they have built up for themselves during their working years. 1 hope it will not be long before we cease making these apologies for pension levels which are below the poverty line and establish the fact that pension levels should in all cases be above the poverty line.
There was also a fair amount of discussion last Wednesday about the methods of indexing which have been used, and it seemed to be agreed by the three of us that indexing has not worked to give our people the level of pension income they require. 1 want to make the point again that the fault is not so much with the system of indexing as it is with the basis upon which we started, or in other words the amount of pension income made available at the beginning. One can take the beginning to be at any time-back in 1926, or in 1952 when we moved from the means test to the principle of universality. Take the beginning at any point and it was never enough; if you establish a basis which is below the requirement for decent living, then no amount of indexing by the rise in the consumer price index will place pensions at a decent level.
I say the time has come to establish a level of pensions below which no one should fall, and that the level should be at least 125 per cent of the figure accepted by Statistics Canada as the poverty or existence level.
During the election campaign we advocated not just an increase in the guaranteed income supplement, as does the bill now before us, but an increase in the basic amount of the old age pension. Whereas the present figure is $35 added to the guaranteed income supplement, we proposed it should have been $40 added to the basic amount.
Some will say right away: that is giving it to a certain number who do not need it. Madam Speaker, that problem is with us all the time. The way to correct it is through adjustments in the Income Tax Act which will take money away in large measure from those who do not need it. In my view, there is a world of difference between making people prove
their poverty in order to get supplements to their pensions and letting people receive the amount and then dealing with it when they file their tax returns. It is also a fact that no matter where you draw the line-I am thinking now of the guaranteed income supplement-there are always many people above that line who are really in a state of poverty.
I did some calculating some years ago-and my recent calculation leads me to believe that the figures stand-that our senior citizens can be grouped into four categories, and for the purpose of simplicity these categories are in round figures. There are three categories of 30 per cent each, and then there is a 10 per cent category at the top. The 30 per cent at the bottom have nothing else, and that is attested to by the fact that they draw the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement. Then there is the 30 per cent group that has something else but not enough, so they draw a portion of the supplement. At the top there is the 10 per cent group whose income is such that they do not need any increase in the old age security, but the way to deal with those people is to increase the amount of income tax a person pays if he or she draws the full old age security benefit.
But in between the 60 per cent level and the 90 per cent level there are 30 per cent of our senior citizens who are really in trouble. They do not get some of the benefits and prerequisites that go with being a recipient of the guaranteed income supplement. They are just over the line. They find it very difficult to see that some of their neighbours who have a little bit less get something additional and are able to carry on while they are stuck in that category. The answer to that whole problem, in our view, is a position we have taken for a long time, namely, that the best thing we ever did was to put old age pensions on a universal basis, and we should get back to that as soon as we can.
I am going to come back to that before I conclude my remarks, but before 1 do so I want to speak about some of the groups that are still left without the consideration and the attention they deserve. That group consists mainly of women who are alone or unattached. A good deal has been said about this $35 supplement that we are going to give now, and are giving in many cases to single women. They get $35, whereas a married couple would only get $17.50 each on a monthly basis. But we are still labouring under what I think is one of the most unfair pieces of social legislation we have ever produced in this country, and that is the spouse's allowance. No amount of trying to fix it up, as the former Liberal government did just before it was defeated or as the Conservative government did while it was in power, got us away from the fact that the spouse's allowance continues to be an unfair arrangement. 1 know this works both ways; it applies to men if they are the younger ones, but there are not that many of them.
According to this arrangement, women in the age bracket 60 to 65 who might be in need get no consideration at all unless they are married to, and living with, an older spouse. The woman in that age bracket who is a widow, divorced or
May 26, 1980

single receives no consideration at all. I know there are a few cases of women in that age bracket who were spouses and were receiving the spouse's allowance but then lost their husbands and now receive the spouse's allowance until they are 65 years of age. That touches only a small part of the problem. That fact that it is done for some widows underlines the fact that any woman who was a widow at the age of 60 or who became a widow before her husband was over 65 does not qualify.
I remember the night when this program was first announced in the election campaign of 1974. I could hardly believe that we were going to bring in a program which would be so discriminatory. It is still there, and I suggest that the time has come to correct that. The only way that it can be corrected is by providing whatever you are going to provide to the spouse between the ages of 60 and 65 without regard to marital status. This business of saying to a woman, "You will get consideration, you will get the pension, you will get the allowance, only if you have a man," does not fit with our thinking today.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
I urge very strongly that the whole business of the spouse's allowance be reviewed. My view is that what we should have instead is a pension available at age 60 to all persons who are out of the labour market. That would catch the single people and the widowed people, whether male or female.
It would do some other things as well. It would encourage many people in that age bracket to retire and thus would open up employment for younger people. I think that is the direction in which we should move. I understand all the talk that goes on against a mandatory retirement age. We do not have a mandatory retirement age in this country by law, but by custom we seem to have it at age 65. I hope to work a lot longer myself-

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
I have already gone seven years beyond that age. 1 press the point as strongly as 1 can that the right to retire when you want to, freedom to make that choice, has far more meaning if you let people retire early than it does if you talk about the right to go on.
For the number of people who want to work beyond 65, there are many times that number, particularly those in the kinds of industries that are in my constituency, people who have a really difficult time keeping up with the rat race, who would like to be able to retire at the age of 60, but they cannot do so if there is not sufficient income. The answer to that, in my view, is to establish a pension at the age of 60, and I would do it both for old age security and the Canada Pension Plan for all those who are out of the labour market.
If the government is not prepared to take that step all at once, if it wants to move part way, then it should impose some kind of an income test between the ages of 60 and 65-

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
A means test?
Old Age Security Act

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
I said income test. The hon. member should not get off the point. I say, do not apply a marital test. If I have to explain it again for the benefit of my hon. friend, there is no question where I stand. I do not want an income test at all. There is no point in suggesting it to the Tories because they would not do it, but I suggest to the government that is over on the other side today that if they want to take one step in that direction, it should be to expand what they are doing, which is a pension provided a woman has a spouse, to a pension provided you are in need of it. Let us get rid of the marital test.
Every time I speak on this subject I speak on behalf of the woman. I know the law works the other way as well, that a man between the ages of 60 and 65 gets the spouse's allowance if his wife is over 65 and gets a pension. There are men who are short changed too because of this legislation, but their number is very few. Custom is such that in most cases the spouse's allowance is being paid to a woman because in most cases she is the one married to the older spouse.
While I am talking about the unfairness of our pension system to women, I want to mention again the fact that the Canada Pension Plan does not have any kind of coverage for homemakers. I want to say right away that I think I understand the Canada Pension Plan very well and I am not suggesting that a pension for homemakers should be made part of the Canada Pension Plan itself. But I do think there should be a parallel plan whereby those women who work in the home and make their contribution to our society and our economy in that way should qualify for benefits equivalent to those that are available to women who are working under the Canada Pension Plan.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
I should say that really the trouble assumes large proportions at about the age of 55. It is women from 55 to 65, especially those who are unattached or alone, who have the greatest difficulty, and one of the reasons for that is that in working years they get lower pay and therefore they build up lower pension rights or, in what might be regarded as their working years, they do the job of a homemaker without any pay, without any pension entitlement, and so this all compounds by the time they reach the age of 55 or 60 and they suffer grieviously, as we all know. There are plenty of statistics about this. Plenty of reports have been written by social agencies of all kinds, by government departments, and of course more reports are being produced all the time. But my contention is that it is time something should be done about it.
As I have said, there are other ways in which women are the victims of ideas that we had in the past, but surely we have got over them. A man and wife live together, raise their family and work. The result of it is that the man goes on a pension and the two of them try to live on that pension, and then the day comes that one of them dies. If the wife dies first, the husband's pension is 100 per cent. But if the husband dies first, the

May 26, 1980
Old Age Security Act
widow's pension in most cases is only 50 per cent of the pension that the two of them had earned by their joint effort both in the home and out in industry. This notion is really for the birds. It has got to go.
One of the places for it to go first should be in the public service. We have done a little better for ourselves as members of Parliament. If a member of Parliament on pension dies, his widow receives 60 per cent. That is a little better than in the public service and in most other employment. But even that, I suggest, is not good enough. Maybe some of the members of Parliament could take a lot less so that the widows could have a better pension.
But apart from that, this is an element of discrimination which just seems to be part of our fabric. It was 50 or more years ago that pension plans were produced in some places where there was no provision for the widow at all. It was a man's world. It has taken decades to get women considered as being entitled to something more than they get just because they happen to be attached to a man. As I say, this means we must do something about a plan that is the equivalent of the Canada Pension Plan for housewives or homemakers. We must do something about this business of the survivor's pension. We must take other steps that I have in mind. This has to apply outside of government. It has to apply to railway pensions, both the CNR and CPR. It has to apply to private pensions. Indeed one thing we need to do in the whole pension field is to take a much closer look at what is going on out there in the private pension world. It is just not good enough, they way things are at the present time.
I said earlier in my remarks that one of the reasons I wanted a guarantee of a pension level to be at least 125 per cent of the poverty level is that our concept has changed about pensions. When pensions were first started in this country as a result of the efforts of my predecessor, the late J. S. Woodsworth, in the middle 1920s and a pension of $20 a month at age 70 was produced, there was great rejoicing. One wonders how there could be rejoicing over that amount. But it was a beginning, and it was brought about in a day when it was felt that if we at least kept the old folks going, we were doing something that was half decent. Surely we have gone beyond that now.
I can remember when we were discussing the Canada Pension Plan in committee a few years ago. One member found certain statistics and he said, "If people get two or three pension plans together, they are going to end up having just as much income in retirement as they had when they were working". This particular member was shocked at the idea. What is wrong with it? If people have helped to build our economy to the point that it produces a certain standard of living, why should our elderly people not have the right to continue to enjoy that standard of living? Therefore, I contend that all of our pension thinking, whether it is the old age security plan itself, the guaranteed income supplement, the Canada Pension Plan, the public service plan, the armed forces plans, the railway plans or private plans, should be geared to the idea of a level of pension that will enable people when they
retire from their productive years to continue to enjoy the standard of living they have had during those years.
It is not often that I go to anything that is connected with the Senate. Hon. members are looking surprised-what have I done? A couple of weeks ago an evening testimonial dinner was held over in Room 200 in the West Block for Senator Croll on the occasion of a report in his name that had been tabled. Actually the party was supposed to have been held earlier this year, but we got into an election and the senators put it off. I went to that party, I admit it. I went to the party for the senator.
1 listened with a great deal of pleasure to the speeches that were made about Senator Croll. I listened to the very good humour that a number of those speakers had, but then I listened with particular delight to David Croll's speech. He is a little older than I, but not much. At least he was talking about a portion of history in this country from the 1920s on with which I am very familiar. I could go along with everything he said in that speech, but as he got toward the end of his speech he said, if I quote him with reasonable correctness, that there are two diamonds in the crown of social legislation that we have built in this country and do not let anyone take away those two diamonds. Now, what were they? One was old age pensions on a universal basis and the other was medicare on a universal basis. Of course, one can imagine that I was ready to stand up and cheer when I heard Senator Croll say that. He elaborated on what it means to our older people to have the guarantee of pensions. I think it is the finest thing we have ever produced in this country, the concept of universality with respect to old age security. I dislike anything that detracts from that universality. I hope we will take heed of the kind of message that Senator Croll gave that night to those who were in Room 200.
There is a lot of talk and a lot of writing these days, a great deal of it misinformed, about pension plans. One reads headlines in the paper which indicate that a great pension robbery is taking place, that the funds will dry up, that we will go into the red, and all that sort of thing. It is a lot of nonsense, really. Let me make my point by saying this: the old age security scheme in this country is the fairest, clearest and most honest pension scheme we have. Why? Those who are working pay in and those who are retired draw their pensions. There is no question about a fund running dry. The pensions are guaranteed by the government and they are paid out of current production. If one is producing, one pays in; if one retires, one draws the pension. It is clear in the case of old age security. The same principle really applied to the Canada Pension Plan.
There is a talk about a fund, but what really counts is the production in any period of time that will make pensions possible. The same is true of all kinds of plans. Let us not get wrapped up in or too concerned about these stories about pension plans being in trouble. We have a basic concept here that is good with old age security on a universal basis. We have the Canada Pension Plan to provide an addition to that so that part of one's retirement income is on an earnings related basis. We have the other things that they can do to improve
May 26, 1980

the picture by taking care of women in the work force, by taking care of spouses and by taking care of widows. If we just give our attention to this, we can have a plan of which we can be really proud.
1 believe as the time goes, mine is just about up, so 1 will not try to go beyond six o'clock. I simply say again that in my view, as one who has followed this subject for half a century, like David Croll, I believe the best thing we have done in Canada is to recognize that our old people on a universal basis deserve the result of the work they have done. Let us put that principle into practice by making our pension of an amount that will enable our older people to live in security and in dignity for the rest of their years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address this House for the first time. I take this opportunity to extend to Madam Speaker, the assistant Speakers and to you, sir, my best wishes and my determination to show a spirit of co-operation throughout Parliament. I am proud to represent the people of Willowdale in our national Parliament, and under different circumstances it would give me a great deal of pleasure to be able to speak about my constituents.
But within the context of this debate on Bill C-16, to increase the Guaranteed Income Supplement for our senior citizens, let me just say this about the people of Willowdale. In my riding there are many senior citizens, many of whom live in homes they built themselves. The people of Willowdale have worked hard to make a contribution to Canada, and they are among the thousands of senior citizens who are watching the passage of this bill with great interest because on July 21 it will mean a few more dollars to help them cope.
For some senior citizens this bill will make it easier to keep their homes, for others it may mean better food and for still others it may mean extra visits to their families. This bill, though, is more important to senior citizens everywhere in Canada. I was pleased to hear in earlier debate that it will receive the support of all parties.
I would like for a moment to examine the broader principles underlying this bill. Canadians are aware of the severe economic challenges confronting all industrialized countries and they realize that Canada is intimately linked to the rest of the world through trade and capital markets. Yet, in the face of fiscal deficits in Canada, and even the possibility of little or no growth this year in our economy, we are increasing this
Old Age Security Act
program of assistance to Canadians in need, a program to which this Liberal government attaches the highest priority.
The philosophy behind this bill was expressed in the throne speech which said:

Canadians recognize the need to live within their national means and they understand that in doing so the state cannot meet every demand or satisfy every group. Therefore, in employing the limited resources available, my ministers will help first those who need help most.

This is a philosophy which I support, because we must strike a balance between fiscal responsibility and assisting those groups in society which are unable to provide for themselves. What does this balance mean to me? It means that, despite the reforms I see as necessary to bring a greater sense of fiscal responsibility to government, it is intolerable that senior citizens are forced to live on incomes which do not provide an acceptable standard of living.
In writing about the plight of the aged, Simone de Beauvoir
said:
We are told that retirement is the time of freedom and leisure: Poets have sung 'the delights of reaching port'. These are shameless lies. Society inflicts so wretched a standard of living upon the vast majority of old people that it is almost tautological to say 'old' and 'poor': Again, most exceedingly poor people are old.
Throughout this debate, Mr. Speaker, it is almost as if aging were a new problem. We have heard the shocking statistics, and we have been told of the terrible plight of one group in particular, elderly women, especially widows and other single women. From all the numbers we have heard it is clear that our senior citizens need help. There is an urgent need for this bill and indeed, for much more than this bill.
1 was glad to hear the minister say in her remarks in this House that this bill was only an interim measure to alleviate the situation of pensioners until greater assistance can be given. Let us therefore look at the context in which pensioners and senior citizens in Canada today are required to provided for their retirement. In particular I should like to discuss pensions and the broader aspects of reform that I perceive to be necessary.
As hon. members are aware, Canada has three basic ways in which it provides retirement income. One is through the Old Age Security Act, of which this GIS is a part. Another is the Canada and Quebec pension plans, and then there are the private pension plans, both those which are employer sponsored and individual plans such as RRSPs.
As hon. members also know, the Canada Pension Plan has problems, the most urgent coming from projections contained in the Lazar and other reports. They show that the Canada Pension Plan funds will be depleted by the end of the century. To make the plan fully funded it is estimated that contributions must be increased from their present rate of 3.6 per cent to 6 per cent first of all, and perhaps to as much as 9 per cent or 11 per cent in the near future.

May 26, 1980
Old Age Security Act
There are, as well, very serious problems with our private pension plans. Less than 40 per cent of the entire working force is covered by private plans and there is little or no protection for part-time labourers, including many women. Figures for 1975 show that 81 per cent of unmarried women, 74 per cent of elderly men and 60 per cent senior couples receive no private pension income based on the work they have done throughout their working lives. In fact Canada has one of the lowest rates of coverage by private plans in the western world. Many of these plans have no portability, and three-quarters of the employer sponsored plans in the private sector require at least ten years of service and/or 45 years of age before pension benefits become those of the people who contributed to them.

Right. 1 cite just one case illustrating the urgent need for portability in our pensions, Mr. Speaker. A woman I know worked for 26 years for a company in Manitoba. That company moved from Manitoba to Saskatchewan, but the woman could not move because of her husband's job in Manitoba. In spite of the money she had invested in her pension plan over 26 years of work, she got only a paltry pension. This is only one example of the many problems of vesting created by our pension plans today and the lack of portability.
As a result of these problems, only 12 per cent of the income of our senior citizens-12 per cent, Mr. Speaker-comes from private pension plans. Nearly half of all income for seniors comes from the public sector, the old age security benefits. I think it is unfortunate that private pension plans have not responded better to modern working conditions. It is estimated that Canadians now change jobs an average of seven times during their working careers. At the same time inflation shows no signs of abating to zero. Pension plans must be designed to react to these realities which working Canadians face every day, if we are to have valuable supplements to the public pension system.
These problems which I have outlined mean that Canadians have less confidence in the private system, less encouragement to save and invest for their future than if a decent return on their investment were assured.
I strongly believe that the pension system will work best when there is a healthy mix of private and public plans. Where possible, people have a responsibility to look after themselves and I endorse the notion that people should save and invest throughout their working years in order to provide for their retirement. But saving and investing will mean nothing if inflation eats into their income and if they lose their contributions because they have changed jobs.

speechtext:
Our current system of providing retirement security for Canadians cries for change and reform. We have 2.3 million seniors today; in 20 years the number will reach 3.4 million, and six to eight million within 50 years. Within 50
years there will be 2.5 times more senior citizens in relation to our working age population than there is at present. We have only a few years now to deal with the dramatic problems that this change in our society, the composition of our work force, is going to create.
Without drastic changes, employer sponsored plans, particularly in the private sector will provide only minimal benefits, locking people into unwanted plans because of onerous vesting provisions, ignoring large parts of the work force, especially women and part time or seasonal workers, and offering little protection against inflation.
The Canada pension plan will become grossly underfunded. The clear message is that Canada will not be able to provide the necessary dollars to meet even the most parsimonious needs of our senior citizens.

I would like to quote from the report of Senator Croll, because I believe it gives an accurate summary of the problem. He said:
It is a tragedy for senior citizens, as well as a blot on the national conscience
that so many old people are being denied a reasonable share of the good things
produced in a wealthy and dynamic society.
The senator went on to say:
It should also be borne in mind that the magnitude of the problem will
certainly increase unless some remedial action is taken.
Mr. Speaker, where are we going now?

I welcomed the announcement in the throne speech of a national pension conference this fall. I was further encouraged when the minister said last Wednesday in this House that a broad cross-section of interested parties, including pensioners, would participate. The national pension conference is one of the ways we can make the phrase "renewed federalism" mean something tangible for senior citizens right across Canada.
I should like to make some comments about the remarks of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), a man who, 1 am glad, and 1 am sure all of us are, to see back in good health and back in opposition because of his very great contributions.
1 do take issue, however, with what he said last Wednesday, and I quote:
When the minister talks about the national pension conference, I gather she sees that as the substitute for legislation.
And then he continued:
An increase of $35 a month does not amount to a pensions policy, nor docs the holding of a conference. The issues have to be dealt with.
I agree that an increase in the GIS is not a policy in itself, and we have not claimed that it is, but I do not think we should dismiss the conference as a substitute for action. It is, rather, as I see it, the spark for action, the start of legislation. 1 think that conference will be very important because it will bring together all those responsible for the pension system- government, private companies and pensioners-"to sit down to work out new directions." This is the best forum to deal
May 26, 1980

with the issues. 1 expect very positive legislation is going to result from this conference.
We have, as others have pointed out, done much of the field work. Now that we have a good idea of the problems, we have to get to work and hammer out the solutions. Without prejudging the results of that conference I should like to make six suggestions.
First, employer sponsored plans must be revised to allow national portability.
Second, private plans must be changed to improve coverage, indexing and adequacy, and private pension plans will have to come up to scratch.
Third, 1 hope the conference will look favourably upon the Croll report recommendation calling for larger contributions to the Canada Pension Plan, otherwise it will be under-funded.
Fourth, the national pension conference will undoubtedly raise important questions about the revenue raising powers of Canada's three levels of government. In this light it is essential to remember that, except for Switzerland, Canada is the most fiscally decentralized of all the countries in the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development.
On the average, tax revenues of local or regional governments among OECD countries are only 44 per cent of that of the federal government. In Canada this figure is 88 per cent.
1 believe that the federal deficit cannot be balanced by fiscal management and restraint alone. The question of fiscal powers must be raised early at a national conference on revenue sharing. It is critical to the building of a new Canadian federalism.
Fifth, Senator Croll recommended against compulsory retirement at age 65. Age does not mean that one is unfit to serve or that one is unfit to work. We must adopt a flexible plan with respect to retirement age.
My final point is one raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who is admired and respected for his work on behalf of retired citizens.

He recommended legislating a pension level of 125 per cent of the poverty line, and made suggestions about the type of indexing that should be used in calculating pensions.
Let me say that I trust that all of us recognize the very real economic needs of our senior citizens. We want to do something for them. The points mentioned are ones that should be at the forefront in our pension conference this fall, and we must find a way to pay for them. This, of course, relates to my point about revenue sharing. Under the current system the federal government would have to bear the full load of any increase. This would be the same with the Canada Pension Plan. The rights of our senior citizens and the funding of the
Old Age Security Act
programs to support them should not be left to the federal government alone.

To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I support enthusiastically the increase in the guaranteed income supplement for senior citizens not only as a necessary measure, but as one which will give rise to a new era of reform.
Our aim must first of all be to enable senior citizens to live in dignity and security without fear of being pursued by poverty every time they go to the supermarket or to the doctor's office.

But, Mr. Speaker, when we have achieved these measures, when we have achieved all these reforms, we will have taken only the first step, that of helping provide financial security for our senior citizens.
The second step, a step even more important than the first, involves a complete change in our attitude toward our senior citizens. They must not be "out of sight, out of mind". They must not be relegated to the ash heap of uselessness. Until we have learned to tap fully the resources of our elderly, their wisdom, their experience, their love and their concern, until we allow seniors a more useful role in our society and until we have taken the second step we, as a nation, will have fallen far short of our great potential.

Mr. Speaker, one way that history rates civilizations is to determine how the old, the physically and mentally disabled have been treated or are treated. When we look at some of the civilizations of the past, we deplore things such as the killing-even though they call it mercy killing-of people who are disabled, sub-normal, crippled or old. Our civilization will be rated by future historians on how we treat our senior citizens and how we treat our crippled and our disabled, whether they are disabled physically or mentally.
I will not be too long tonight because I know there are many other members who want to make a contribution to this debate, but I do want to deal with about five or six items that come under the principle of this bill.
The first one was dealt with by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) under the topic of universality. There was a time when I was very vocal in regard to universality, and I felt that the pension was the right of citizenship and that everyone should receive it. I have changed my mind, for two reasons. In the first place, the government is short of funds. The government has to establish priorities. When priorities are established, it is not always that senior citizens or the disabled who get high enough on the list.
When I enter a home of a senior citizen who has worked his entire life in a coal mine, I find that in the last three days of the month that person has to eat bread and soup occasionally because his pension has run out. Then I look at those who are in that upper group, the 10 per cent or 15 per cent of people who do not need money at all. Even though they pay some
1406

May 26, 1980
Old Age Security Act
back in income taxes, they do not put it all back. Because of these two things I have come to a conclusion that a better policy than universality would be to keep the same amount of money for this particular vote but to distribute it on a different basis so that those who needed it would get it, and those who do not require it at all would not get it.
I know there are many people who are over the age of 65 who have not applied for the old age pension, and properly so in my view. They do not need it, they are still working. I can see no reason to pay a pension to people who are still working. We talk about leaving the choice of retirement at age 65 or at whatever age a person wants to retire. That fits right into my philosophy of life, freedom of choice, which is part of the philosophy of the party I represent in this House. But if we are going to say that people who are able and who want to will continue to earn wages well past the age of 65, then 1 can see no reason at the same time to be paying them a pension out of public funds because they are senior citizens. I would much rather that that money be distributed to those who need it so that our senior citizens will not have to live during the last four or five days of the month on dry bread or watered-down soup.
We have to be realistic about dealing with this matter of universality. I can see no reason to pay the pension to those who are well off and who are well able to live without it and, at the same time, not pay enough to those who really need it so that those people can at least live reasonably well through the period in which that pension is paid.
I have changed my mind about the pension being a right of citizenship. I do not want to go back into any rigid poverty means test. I simply say that those who are working and continuing to earn good wages after 65 should not, in my view, be drawing the old age pension. That money, whatever amount, would bring into the pockets of those who really need it a little bit of extra cheer, without costing the government any more if the priority prevents the government from increasing the amount of money for this particular vote.
The second item that I want to deal with is directly in connection with the guaranteed income supplement as set out in this bill. During the election there was a good deal of misunderstanding. Many people said, "we will be getting S35 each after the election if Mr. Trudeau is elected." According to my understanding of the bill, that was right. I said, "yes, I believe that is what is planned." It has been rather sad for many married couples to find that it is $35 per household, or $17.50 each. It will certainly be helpful and help those who are having a difficult time, but it is another aspect that I do not like.
One married couple said to me, and I was horrified when they said it, "We could very easily separate and get $35 each." I hope the department will keep very close tab on that particular item. The laws of this country should be encouraging marriage, not separation, or common law which is becoming more acceptable and more common in many areas.
In my view we should be sticking to the family which is the foundation of this nation, encouraging the family to stick together, work together, and, as 1 often said, pray together. When we pay so much per household, it has an adverse effect. When we pay $17.50 each to a married man and a married woman, both of whom are pensioners, and pay $35 to a bachelor, it does make our senior people think.
I would like the government to think that problem through and see if there is something that can be done to do away with this aspect that many people feel is discriminatory. They are all old age pensioners, yet they are being paid different amounts. Many of them have the same expenses, the same rent and everything else, but they get a different amount of money. I hope that our legislation will not drive married people apart but will be aimed at keeping them together to the greatest degree possible.
The third item I want to deal with in connection with this bill has already been mentioned by other speakers, that is, those who do not qualify at all. They feel that this is discrimination. Take the spinster who is 58 years of age. When she reaches 61 or 62, she still gets nothing. She has to wait until she is 65 before she can get any assistance.
What about the widow whose husband died when she was 58 and he was 59? She has raised her family and now she is alone. She will get nothing until she is 65. This is a sad group, an unfortunate group to be in. Such a person would look at her sister or brother who happens to be married, and would see that they get enough at least to keep them alive. Some of these people feel bitter. Some have said, "Why didn't the spinster who worked all her life provide for her old age?" There are many reasons. Many of these people are spinsters because they were providing for a widowed mother or a disabled father, or for a brother or sister who was unable to look after themselves. They sacrificed their life earning and providing and keeping a home through all those years, until they suddenly found that they were old. But for them there is no help until they are 65.
Rather than universality, giving something to everybody, 1 hope that we will try to give something, even though it is not the greatest possible amount, to those who need it. There are those who have planned for the future who today are having a nightmare of frustration. They worked hard all their lives, built up a farm or a business, and now they are ready to retire. They think they have enough put aside. They paid taxes throughout the years. Now they feel they are able to retire and live on what they have provided for themselves.
When they go to sell their farm or their business, the government steps in and says, "Just a minute, we want half of that to be taxed as capital gains." They have already paid their taxes throughout the years, paid it on every cent they have made. They have been scrupulously honest. Now their government is taking another handful.
It has reached the point where one farmer in my riding said to me, "Now I am on the poverty line, all my plans have been cast aside because this capital gains stuff came in." It not only kills initiative, but it ruins the hopes and the plans of people who have built and worked long hours and long days, in many
May 26, 1980

cases without holidays. They did this in order to build up something for their old age, but now they find there is not enough there.
One of the last speakers mentioned inflation. If we need to have capital gains, and 1 do not think we do-I would like to see it done away with entirely-why do we include the inflationary aspect when we start to value capital gains? A businessman said to me he would not have minded paying on the true capital gains, but he had to pay on the inflated value. We index pensions but we do not index capital gains. There has to be some fairness in this. If capital gains were eliminated, many businesses would expand. Many senior citizens would be able to retire. If this were to happen on the farm, a young man could farm more land, raise more cattle and more food. It would be a boon to the economy. As long as we keep capital gains over the heads of people, they are not going to use that initiative.
As I think I told this House before, one businessman said to me, "I'll work 14 hours a day to build up something for my wife and my children, but I am not going to work 14 hours a day to build up something for some blankety-blank government." He was not referring to any particular stripe of government, just government which would take part of the earnings he built up for his old age. Well, they did plan, but it hasn't worked out. Small businessmen face the same thing.
Small business-the last member spoke feelingly about encouraging business to provide a pension plan of some type- is faced with the problem of just staying alive without including anything else. If we are to have pension plans in our small businesses there has to be some government encouragement, not government help but government encouragement. Just look at the figures presented by the government the other day. There were 5,000 bankruptcies in the month of April alone. Five thousand businesses went under; those were businesses without any retirement plan. It is said that the best of plans sometimes go astray, and I can feel the bitterness from some of our people who have planned and worked only to find that through no fault of their own they are left in a precarious position in the senior years of their lives.
The next point I would deal with is the matter of social legislation. In this country we are getting to the point at which we are including everything under social legislation, including veterans pensions and pensions for prisoners of war. Veterans pensions should not be under social legislation, neither should pensions for prisoners of war, veterans and their dependants. That is not social legislation. That is a national obligation. These people left part of their lives on the battlefields so that we could live a life in freedom with our own government. Then we put them under social legislation. It is not social legislation at all. It is a national obligation. We say we will pay so much to widows of pensioners who were getting less than 47 per cent, down to 37 per cent, so that in five years they will be able to get their proper pension. Mr. Speaker, I wonder if it is realized how old these people are. Some of them served in World War
Old Age Security Act
I, and others in World War II. They haven't long to live. We say to the widows, "Wait for another four years and then you will get the pension your husband would have received had he lived." I do not think we should include veterans and prisoners of war under social legislation at all. It is a number one national obligation which we owe to these people.
The last point I want to mention concerns the way in which we work out pensions. It is a type of universality, I suppose. To get back to the point with which I started tonight, I think history will decide whether we are in the high category, the medium category or the low category when we are being rated according to the way we treat our senior citizens. I am not referring to the rich; they can look after themselves. I am concerned with those who are not able to look after themselves, those who made plans which went astray, or those who did not make plans but who are human beings, and the group of women who are in that category but who get nothing until they are 65. They are too old to work so we tell them to go on welfare after they have spent their lives saving money for the government because they continued to work to look after a disabled brother, mother or father.
I will support the second reading of this bill although I do not like the division of the $35 a month between a married couple. I think it is going to drive some families apart. But every bit helps. I went into a home in my riding. A man who spent 50 years working in the coal mines was eating dry bread.
1 felt a lump come into my throat: after all those years, this fine man who raised a family, could only afford to eat dry bread. He did not have any money left from his pension. We can do better than we are doing. If the government cannot find extra dollars to help these people, let us forget about the extra 10 per cent or 15 per cent at the top, those who don't need the money. Let us distribute that amount, at least, to those who are in dire need. We will be helping to raise the poverty line. Let us make sure that when history rates us we won't be at the bottom of the ladder.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to participate in the debate on the second reading of Bill C-16. I must also say, that I feel very close to this issue. As many hon. members may know, I was a family physician before the last election. But what they may not know is that my practice was largely dealing with the elderly. So you see, Mr. Speaker, I feel I have a good first-hand knowledge of the problems faced by the elderly as they relate to health and also social security measures.
I think every hon. member realizes the gravity of the problem of maintaining a decent standard of living for our senior citizens. The situation is especially acute in times like the present when governments must walk a fine line in terms of aiding those hurt by inflation and of fuelling the fires of inflation through increased government spending. In the Speech from the Throne it was recognized that, "Inflation strikes hardest at the aged and those least able to take care of themselves." It is precisely in view of this that the government

May 26, 1980
Old Age Security Act
is proceeding early with the proposal to raise the guaranteed income supplement by $35 a month.
There is no doubt that there is a real need for increased assistance to our elderly population. 1 would like to illustrate this fact with a few startling statistics. As many in this House may know, we have in our country approximately two million persons currently receiving the basic old age security pension. But what many may not be aware of, however, is the extent to which these old age pensioners rely on the government to provide additional income assistance through the GIS program. For example, over a half of all old age pensioners have little or no income apart from the basic pension. In December, 1979, 807,000 elderly persons were receiving a partial income supplement. Even more indicative of the vulnerability of our older population is the fact that an additional 381,000 were receiving the maximum benefit payable under the guaranteed income supplement. In other words, about 17 per cent of all pensioners rely solely on the federal government to provide them with the income they require.
The minister has indicated that we are falling short of the mark in guaranteeing our elderly population an income which is at least equal to the poverty level. I say that this is only the first step in bringing our elderly just up to the poverty level. This is only a first step and I support the legislation before us for that reason. The poverty level particularly affects single pensioners, and they are predominantly women. It is in an effort to bring these people closer to that mark-the mark of the poverty level, that they may live their later years in some semblance of dignity and independence-that we are seeking approval of Bill C-16 today.
Bill C-16 is not a complex piece of legislation. In general, the bill directs additional financial assistance to the low income, elderly population and, in particular, to single elderly people, who do not benefit from the combined effects of two OAS pensions and two GIS benefits.
The GIS rates, established under the Old Age Security Act, are adjusted quarterly, in accordance with the consumer price index. The maximum rate, for the quarter commencing April 1, 1980, is $153.35 a month for a single pensioner, and $127.51 a month each for a couple where both are pensioners. Up to these rates, the amount of GIS payable depends on the pensioners' monthly income from other sources. Bill C-16 provides that, in addition to the normal indexation made for the quarter commencing July 1, 1980, the maximum monthly GIS rates will be further increased by $35 for a single pensioner, and $17.50 each for a pensioner couple, or $35 per pensioner household. This increased benefit will be subject, to the normal quarterly cost of living increases, Mr. Speaker.
The proposed amendment to increase GIS and SPA benefits will provide an additional $35 per month for each household receiving GIS, or GIS and spouse's allowance payments. For a two pensioner couple receiving GIS, or an OAS-GIS pensioner with a spouse receiving SPA, the increase will be $17.50 on each monthly cheque. Single recipients will receive $35 more
each month. The larger proportional increase for unattached pensioners recognizes the fact that basic costs for one person, living alone, are proportionately greater than the expenses for two persons living together.
The Department of National Health and Welfare estimates that, as a result of this bill, an additional 45,000 pensioners and spouses will become entitled to partial GIS and SPA benefits. With the rise in the maximum GIS and SPA levels, these persons, whose other income was too high previously to qualify for GIS or SPA benefits, will now become eligible for a monthly benefit of up to $35. As well, Mr. Speaker, OAS pensioners and spouses whose income level is too high to qualify for GIS or SPA, will not be affected by the increase.
It is important to note that this proposed increase will be in addition to the regular quarterly indexation made in accordance with changes in the consumer price index. In essence, the proposal represents an increase in the real value of the GIS and SPA benefits of all eligible recipients.
In total, there will be an increase of approximately $345 million in the hands of low income, elderly Canadians for the balance of the 1980-81 fiscal year, and approximately $525 million in 1981-82, the first full fiscal year for which the increase is in effect. In terms of the estimated number of elderly recipients benefiting from the increase, the figure for 1980-81 is 1,379,000, and for 1981-82, 1,443,000. The bottom line, of course, is the amount of expenditure in total that the government is allocating toward meeting the needs of senior citizens. The figures for total spending in the old age security, guaranteed income supplement and spouse's allowance programs for 1980-81 are $7.5 billion, and for 1981-82 $8.5 billion.
So, as you can see, Mr. Speaker, the government is directing a very considerable portion of its budget as part of a continuing commitment to the elderly. The $35 increase in the GIS is a much needed and significant step on the road to providing more economic security for senior citizens. In view of this I am sure members opposite will be delighted to support a measure which helps assuage the vulnerability of older people living on fixed incomes.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address my comments to future problems relating to income security for the aged. The government has already taken steps in this direction by calling for a national pension conference in the fall, but I firmly believe that we must act with the greatest dispatch in addressing this problem. At present, Canadians over 65 constitute approximately 8.7 per cent of our population. In 20 years this figure will rise to 13 per cent, and by 2031 it is estimated it will hit 20 per cent, almost three times the figure at present. As well, the ratio of Canadians aged 65 and over to those aged 20 to 65 is 15.60 per cent-that is more than six workers per pensioner. By the year 2031 this ratio will be 33.37 per cent, or less than three workers for every pensioner. So it would appear that the tax burden of the Canada Pension Plan will more than double in the next 50 years. The time to act on this problem is now, Mr. Speaker.
May 26, 1980

I think a good starting point from which to initiate discussion is the Report of the Task Force on Retirement Income Systems. While the report does not make specific recommendations, it does outline a broad range of policy alternatives that might be considered to upgrade the system. The main findings of the report are outlined in relation to the two main objectives that underlie the current pension system. These are: first, to alleviate poverty among the elderly; and second, to assist and/or require people to defer consumption during their working years through taxes, pension contributions and savings in order to ensure that the living standards they experience during their work years are maintained adequately after retirement.
Among the findings of the study were that only 48 per cent of workers were members of employer sponsored pensions plans in 1976. Many of these will never collect an adequate pension because most plans are not portable. Rules regarding an employee's right to ownership of pension credits, known as vesting, are too stringent. Moreover, the after tax income of the elderly is only about 40 per cent of younger persons. For example, in 1975 average elderly income was $4,620 after tax; compared with $11,870 for the non-elderly.
The report also notes that more than half of Canada's retired persons collecting pensions also receive guaranteed income supplements, additional benefits paid to needy pensioners. It is stated in the report:
This makes clear that many people who were not in financially tight circumstances during their working lives find themselves in that situation after retirement.
As well, it states that the Canadian employer sponsored pension system is behind most other western industrialized countries in terms of coverage and vesting provisions.
Another of the findings was that fewer than half of workers with employer sponsored plans have survivor benefits, leaving widows without any extra support in their later years.
Also, up to one half of middle-income earners making between $12,000 and $24,000 will see a significant drop in living standards after retirement unless the public and private pension system is reformed. In addition, it says government could provide more subsidized housing for the elderly, and raise old age pension and supplementary benefits payments based on wage increases.
The report also proposes compulsory establishment of an earnings related plan on an indexed scale, possibly through expansion of the Canada Pension Plan. The CPP, which pays a monthly pension of about $244 to contributors and their survivors, is based on earnings.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to dwell for a moment on the issue of health care delivery for the elderly. I believe it is an integral part of a comprehensive package of security for our senior citizens. When we are talking about financial security for senior citizens, we have to consider the total social security for senior citizens. As 1 have mentioned, this has been an area of vital interest to me. As the percentage of people over 65 increases, we will be faced with a vast array of problems relating to health, aging, poverty,
Old Age Security Act
institutionalization, isolation and depression. In my view the health care system must be sensitive to the special needs of our senior citizens and adapt to these needs rather than having the elderly adapt to the needs of the health care system.
None of what 1 have just said is new, since health care officials and the public have been aware of the problem for years. But time is catching up with us, and this awareness must be translated very soon into action.
To sum up, the same applies to the need to reform the system of retirement income. While Bill C-16 helps to redress some of the immediate financial difficulties now being experienced by segments of our elderly population, we must direct our efforts, in consultation and co-operation with the provinces, toward finding a long-term solution to this problem.

Madam Speaker, 1 would like to make a few comments about what has been said on that very important legislation. My colleagues will no doubt support the policy of income supplement for a group of individuals for whom we have the highest respect and consideration. I think that we are dealing with people who deserve the attention of all hon. members not out of charity but respect for the contribution they have made to our history and life as many others have. I am not speaking on behalf of the thousands of unemployed but of those who are enjoying a well-earned retirement. Most of them are very concerned and are experiencing some problems because benefits have not kept pace with the cost of living increases, as measured by the consumer price index.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to repeat how pleased 1 am to say a few words about that proposal, but I am not convinced that if there had not been elections last February such amendment would have been made so early. One thing I would like to say is that, as a government, we had made a commitment. The former minister had already shown his interest in discussing all these social issues at a conference with the provinces. Also, in reply to questions asked, he undertook to initiate a full review of the hardships of our senior citizens. Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief, of course. I know there is a hope or a tendency to proceed with this bill in Committee of the Whole and possibly even third reading later this evening. 1 do not know if that is possible, but it is certainly desirable. I think all of us realize the importance of passing this bill since its benefits would be made available to senior citizens come July 1.
When I first arrived in this House many years ago, it seemed to me that the whole concept of pensions was much simpler. It was based on the concept of universality. I look with a certain amount of misgiving, perhaps, at the trend away from universality. It concerns me. I read the minister's speech last Wednesday, and it was an excellent speech. There were two things in that speech which impressed me. One, of course, is the minister's intention to bring together all the people in this country who are interested in the total concept of pensions-not simply old age pensions but also industrial pensions-with particular emphasis on the private sector, at a conference this fall or perhaps next spring.
It will be interesting if, coming out of that conference, can be some new concepts or, perhaps better still, a return to the basic concept of universality. It seems to me that it should not be too difficult to combine universality with the Income Tax Act to make certain that the number of people who benefit or obtain pensions, G1S or what have you and who do not really need this kind of income, would find it simply retrieved by the government through the income tax system.
One very persuasive member talked tonight about the need of a means test to make certain that the money goes only to the people who need it. This is a laudable concept, but I have yet to see anybody in the public service, the opposition or in my own party in caucus come up with a system or method of determining need or means properly. 1 have heard the argument that the need of a senior citizen living in Toronto, Vancouver or Montreal may be greater, theoretically, than that of a person living in a smaller community in New Brunswick or Nova Scotia. This is why I retreat a little from discussing the poverty line. What is the poverty line? It is certainly not uniform in this country.
I think statistics would indicate that the poverty line in one part of the country is different from that in another part of the country, so the whole matter becomes more and more complicated, more and more formulae are devised, and more and more bureaucracy is introduced, with more and more regulations. Why? Because we do not have the courage in this House of Commons to say that we are going back to universality and
Old Age Security Act
that really the whole pension plan needs improvement, and not just the GIS.
People have argued eloquently for the need for de-regulation, and I agree. We are an over-regulated society, but regulations usually come in because of a lack of restraint and willingness to make regulations unnecessary. When we depart in the slightest from the concept of universality, we are automatically increasing the bureaucracy and automatically increasing the number of regulations. Once someone says the money should go only to those who need it most, we are automatically setting up regulations, if only to determine who are the people who need it most. This has always eluded the better brains in the public service, so I am rather anxious to see the outcome of this particular badly needed conference to see if somehow we might want to get back to the concept of universality.
This, of course, does not ignore the fact that thousands of Canadians, because of hard work, because of a rich father or because of a relatively illness-free lifetime-for a lot of reasons-reach the age of 60, 65 or 70 when they desire to retire from the work force without any need of an old age pension. However, it seems to me that the logical way of retrieving or getting that money back is through the income tax system and not through having bureaucrats crawling over our bank books, peering under our beds and all the rest of it, to see whether we are actually in need. I am not exaggerating because this really was one of the characteristics of the depression days when we were very, very meticulous about making certain that nobody got something unless he or she could demonstrate it was deserved as a result of the sweat on his or her brow, as they used to say. It bothers me slightly that we seem to be getting away from the concept of universality.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said at the beginning of her speech:
The federal government is not the only source of financial assistance to elderly Canadians. It is fair to say that more and more provinces are introducing supplementary programs to assist elderly Canadians. Does this bill affect such programs and what is the relationship between the provincial programs and the federal program?
It seems that there is a parallel or relationship between what the minister asked in that question and the experiences which we are now running into in the medicare plan. Medicare has been one of the greatest contributing factors to the well-being and quality of life of people in this country. If we look at the medicare plan in the United States, we will see that it does not come anywhere near the Canadian plan. There is no universality and, indeed, no plan.
We pride ourselves on the universality of medicare. But just a couple of years ago we introduced the concept of block funding, which is leading away from universality and from a common standard across this country. What has happened as a result of block funding? We need only look at the medicare plan in Ontario but, more important, as people study the results of block funding in medicare, we are finding that it perpetuates regional disparity. It is obvious that certain prov-

May 26, 1980
Old Age Security Act
inces are unable to match the quality or standard of medicare found in other provinces, particularly the have-provinces. I can think of, for example, Nova Scotia's plan, with which I am familiar because I recently studied it.
Once again, unintentionally of course, we have a policy which perpetuates regional disparity. My party, the Liberal party, has been able to forge a marriage of convenience between private enterprise and government. We believe that the private enterprise system of this country is the greatest generator of capital in the history of this country or of the world. Private industry is by far the most successful generator of capital. We need capital in this country, not only to provide jobs, but to provide a quality of life. We are talking tonight about senior citizens, but tomorrow we could be talking about equality of opportunity in the educational system for young people.
The marriage of convenience between private enterprise and the government is that the government insists on having some input into the distribution of some of that capital in order to provide a standard of living for all Canadians. It is only when the two partners, as in any marriage, fight over the income that the marriage has tremendous strains put upon it. Over the last ten years we have run into that situation. Private industry is, quite properly, demanding more of the available funds, and those who believe in social reform are unwilling to give a little.
Consequently, concepts are evolved by harrassed public servants in an attempt to break the conflict. So we end up with, in the case of old age pensions, a retention of the concept of universality, supplemented by guaranteed income supplement and by provincial contributions. The end result is that the changes are made in the GIS and not in the basic income. Again, it could be retrieved through income tax, particularly in these days of computerization.
What concerns me is the trend toward a continuation of regional disparity. Sooner or later senior citizens living in a have-not province, and we never know which province that may be in five years or ten years' time, cannot expect to have the same income as senior citizens in Quebec or Ontario. And it is wrong to presume that it costs any less to live in the Atlantic provinces than it costs to live in the city of Montreal. If rent is less, then food is more expensive, transportation is more expensive, and medicare is more expensive. Really, there is no big difference. If anything, the cost of living is probably greater in the Atlantic provinces than in the central provinces.
Yet, senior citizens over time, if not already in some provinces, will obtain from the various levels of government considerably more income than somebody in the less favoured regions of the country. I suspect that this is why the minister said that she hopes that the provinces would not attempt to retrieve some of the money from the $35 under one pretext or another.
The minister also said that she was pleased to be advised that Nova Scotia and British Columbia will be passing on the full increase to all GIS recipients. However, some of the other provinces may not pass on this increase. If they do not, then the senior citizens in those provinces will have less income than
those in Nova Scotia or British Columbia. Thus we begin again the whole cycle of accentuating the differences in our country rather than, at this very important time in our history, going the other way.
What must come out of our constitutional talks, whether they be next month or three years or four years from now, is a dedication to certain basic principles. Those principles could be perhaps summed up by simply saying "equal opportunity for all Canadians". Equal opportunity for all Canadians means access to the same facilities right across the country, such as education, medicare, income for senior citizens, and family allowances. When we in this House allow ourselves to depart from this basic principle, perhaps to accommodate some of the provinces or to appease other provinces, or perhaps even because of some conflict over what confederation is all about, what we have done, unintentionally I am sure, is to put in place programs which help some people and not others.
Somebody said earlier today that a certain amount of jealousy is built into the programs, that if it is not $35 for most people, then it is $17.50. It is $35 for a household, but it is only a matter of time before there will be regional differences and regional jealousy. Such a disparity will have the effect of encouraging people, once more, to leave the have-not provinces for the more favoured provinces. It is happening now in Quebec, to some degree. People there who are in their sixties are leaving because inheritance taxes and duty taxes are different. These people are planning their estates and saying, "As much as I would like to remain in this province, maybe 1 would like to move into Ontario. It is still part of Canada, but I want to go there because of the taxes."

Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to congratulate you on your appointment to the position which you now hold, and I do so. I should also like to congratulate the minister on her appointment. In her
